content.thinking:
I'm checking the sandbox directory structure before planning the design. For the elf ranger archer, I'm thinking roughly 1.85m tall, anime heroic style, slim and elegant, with a neutral A-pose or T-pose for readability — arms extended sideways with limbs clearly separated.

I'm working through how to pose the bow: holding it vertically in the left hand while the arm rests in an A-pose would make the bow extend beyond the model's head height, throwing off proportions. I'm weighing alternatives like slinging the bow on the back with the quiver versus holding it diagonally or lower in the hand to keep the overall height and silhouette clean for rigging.

Right, the bow curves with limbs tipping back toward the archer while the belly faces the target, so I'll place it in the YZ plane at roughly x=0.74, building the limb shape with a curved sweep and a thin string rod stretched between the tips; I'll leave the right hand empty and open rather than nocking an arrow, saving the quiver for the back.

For the overall design I'm settling on a tall anime-proportioned elf ranger, around 8 heads high, with a hood-down cloak, flowing cape, long braided hair, leaf-shaped pauldron, bracers, trimmed leather tunic, greaves, and a belt with pouches and a dagger, using a forest green and teal palette with gold accents.

Now I'm pinning down the color palette: silvery-white hair with a greenish tint, emerald-amber eyes, light elven skin tone, deep green cloth, a cream-lined cloak with gold trim, and layered brown leathers in varying shades. With that settled, I'm starting to lay out the character's joint skeleton for the SDK, beginning with the hip root and spine chain.

I'm working through body proportions for a roughly 1.84-unit-tall figure -- placing ankles, knees, hips, pelvis, waist, chest, shoulders, neck, and head positions, with elongated legs and a slightly oversized anime-style head, leaving room for pointed ears and hair to extend just past the crown.

Now I'm settling on an overall height near 1.86, narrowing the shoulder and waist width for a slender elf build, and deciding to define joints using explicit world-space coordinates (with "L" marking the left side, x = +1) to avoid confusion with local frame conventions. I'm setting up the leg stance with feet slightly apart and turned out, using a limb-building approach from hip to ankle.

Working out the leg joint chain -- placing hip, knee, and ankle targets so the leg bends slightly forward naturally, then structuring the kneeL and ankleL joints along that path with the ankle as the chain's tip before adding foot joints.

Still defining the foot chain...

Now moving to arms: shoulder, upper arm, elbow, wrist, hand, fingers, with an A-pose angled roughly 35° below horizontal outward, setting upper arm length to 0.29, forearm to 0.27, and hand to 0.18.

I'm working out the arm chain positions, placing shoulders at roughly ±0.2, 1.49, and computing the left arm's bent elbow and raised forearm for the bow-holding pose using direction vectors.

Then I'm sizing the bow itself relative to the grip point, aiming for a longbow around 1.3-1.4 meters that fits below head height, with tips spanning roughly 0.45 to 1.8 in height.

Now I'm working out the fist and finger geometry: the palm wraps around the vertical grip axis, with fingers curling around it as curved chains. Planning each hand with a palm box plus four finger chains of a few joints each keeps the total joint count for both hands around 25, well within budget.

I'm defining a hand-building approach using a local frame derived from the wrist-to-fingertip direction, palm normal, and cross axis, then placing finger bases and curling segments along those vectors for either an open hand or a gripping fist.

I need to reconsider the grip orientation: for the fist to wrap around a vertical bow grip, the fingers' curl axis must be vertical, meaning the hand should be oriented horizontally like gripping a vertical pole, rather than curling in the plane I originally assumed.

Let me try a concrete arm pose instead: elbow bent, forearm extending forward and slightly outward, with the hand pointing forward so the fingers can wrap naturally around the grip.

Checking the proportions though, holding the bow fully extended forward puts it too high relative to the body, so I should shorten the bow length or lower the grip point. For an A-pose, I want the arms angled outward from vertical rather than straight down or straight out, so I'm adjusting the shoulder and elbow positions to get roughly a 35-degree spread.

I'm working through whether the hand orientation actually matches a natural grip on a vertical object — with the wrist pointing down and outward, the curl axis doesn't align for wrapping a vertical shaft, so I'm testing whether flexing the wrist forward or treating it like holding a staff at one's side with a hammer grip gives a more physically plausible pose.

Working through the geometry, I'm placing the grip so fingers curling toward -X wrap around its front side, positioning the bow center relative to the wrist-to-hand offset and checking the span against the bow's length.

Now I'm sketching the arm chain for the bow-holding side: shoulder to elbow to wrist positions, deriving hand and grip coordinates from that, and roughing out upper-arm and forearm direction vectors by normalizing and scaling rather than solving full IK. Then I move to the opposite arm, planning it open-handed and angled outward similarly.

I'm also working out the torso: building a spine chain from hips through spine joints to chest using a catmull path, treating hips as the root joint since it has no parent, then deciding how to structure the loft/sweep for the body silhouette using ellipse radii along that chain.

For the head, I'll work in world coordinates to avoid confusion over local axes, placing the head center around (0,1.72,0.02) and sizing the skull as a scaled sphere for that anime elf look.

I'm shaping the cranium as a scaled sphere and adding a separate smaller sphere for the jaw/chin area to form a pointed, tapered chin, keeping the combined surface smooth enough for eye decals to project cleanly onto.

For eyes, I'll place anime-style eye decals symmetrically around the front of the face using a surface projection helper, then shape the head with low-poly ellipsoid combinations and add long, pointed elf ears extruded from a leaf-like outline.

Working out the ear geometry now, defining an outward-back-up axis direction and the perpendicular plane needed to extrude a flat, tapered ear shape...

I derive the thickness axis as the component of the normal perpendicular to the ear's long axis, then move on to defining the actual leaf-shaped outline points for the ear geometry.

For hair I'm planning a silver, anime-style look using a hair cap mesh scaled over the skull with a face opening, plus separate extruded locks for bangs, and adding small touches like a gold ear cuff for detail.

I also need to check that the hair cap's bottom edge doesn't creep too far down the sides, since it's wider there, and verify it won't cover the sideburn/cheek area near the jaw. Checking the ellipsoid cross-section at the eye level x-position confirms the hair stays clear of the face front where the eyes sit.

Since the skull only barely protrudes past the hair, I think it's safer to cut a frontal opening in the hair sphere using the sphere geometry's phi/theta start and length parameters, carving out a 120°-wide front sector so the face shows through properly.

But I realize a cut shell sphere has a thin visible edge at the opening since it's single-sided, which could look odd—though since it sinks slightly outside the skull it should be mostly fine. For a proper hairline shape like a widow's peak, I think bangs made from separate geometry might work better than just carving the sphere.

I'm trying to figure out the right theta ranges for splitting the hair into a top cap and a side/back cap so the boundary lines up correctly with the forehead at roughly y=1.76-1.81, matching eyebrow placement—though stitching two spherical caps together at their edges seems messy, so a lathe-based approach might be cleaner.

Adjusting the sideburn angle to ±55° for a more realistic hairline, I'll exposes cheeks between hair and face. For the front I'm planning two long side locks framing the face down to the chest, plus pointed fringe locks across the forehead, and a tapered braided ponytail chain running down the back to the waist.

For the overall structure, I'm sketching torso proportions as a loft with stations from pelvis through waist, chest, shoulders, and neck base, defining width and depth at each height to shape the tunic form.

I'll simplify by making the torso loft serve double-duty as the tunic itself—greenish and bigger than the body—with a separate skin-toned sweep just for the neck, keeping bare arms handled separately.

Working out the sleeve and accessory details: short green tunic sleeves to the elbow with cream undersleeves and leather bracers, a baldric strap crossing the chest to hold a back quiver, a pouched belt with a dagger, and a single leaf-shaped leather pauldron with gold trim on the left shoulder.

For the cape, I'm defining it as a membrane stretched between a shoulder-line edge and a lower hem edge, draping behind the back and curving down to calf-length while making sure the geometry stays clear of the torso.

Mapping out the cloak's neckline and hem as curved point paths, with the front clasp anchoring the mantle where it drapes over the shoulders down to the chest.

I realize the straight interpolated lines between those edges would intersect the arms in the A-pose, so I'm narrowing the cloak to hang mainly behind the back and over the shoulders rather than across the front where the arms sweep through.

For skinning, I'm considering whether to rigidly bind the cape to the chest bone or smooth it between spine joints so the hem trails naturally below the hips rather than snapping stiffly with the torso. I also want to add a draped hood piece around the neck, like a lathe-generated cowl shape sitting behind the collar.

Now I'm planning the hood as a flattened ellipsoid pile sitting on the shoulders at the back of the neck, then moving on to legs: tight trousers with a tapered thigh sweep, boots with gold trim and a folded cuff at the knee, and a toe shape built from a capsule-like loft for the foot.

I'm defining the radius function along the hip-knee-ankle sweep path, tapering from a wider thigh to a narrower ankle, and splitting the leg into color bands so pants cover the upper portion and the boot takes over just below the knee with a cuff ring marking the transition.

Now I'm settling the painting approach: using cel-shaded paints with ink outlines for cuffs and gold-toned cel for metallic details, reserving flat colors for small accents like strings, and keeping the palette within roughly 20 flat colors while painted surfaces share a texel density based on total painted area.

I'll stick with a 1024 paint sheet rather than 2048, since for a 1.85 m figure with ~6 m² of painted area that still gives about 2.9 mm texel density, plenty fine for crisp cel edges without risking atlas bloat from other textures like eyes and cards.

Now I'm sketching the quiver for the back — a tilted leather cylinder roughly 0.55 m long and 0.065 m radius, with gold bands and straps.

I'm working out the arrow placement, with six arrows sticking up from the quiver's mouth showing feathered fletching and small svg-based arrowheads. For orientation, since the bow is in the left hand and the draw hand is the right, the quiver should angle with its top near the right shoulder and its bottom near the left hip, though I'll need to check whether the cape ends up covering it.

Now I'm resolving a depth conflict between the cape and quiver — if the cape hangs full-length it intersects the quiver's position, so I'm considering an asymmetrical half-cloak draped only over the left shoulder (bow-arm side) while the quiver sits openly on the right side of the back, avoiding overlap.

I'll span the cape from the left shoulder diagonally down to mid-back, with a long trailing gold-trimmed hem reaching toward the calf, attached under a left pauldron with a clasp, while the right shoulder carries the quiver's strap plus a bracer. Now I'm mapping out the specific coordinates for the cape's top edge and hemline to get the drape and silhouette right.

Checking the cape curve stays clear of the torso and quiver placement as it drapes down the back, verifying the z-depth offsets at chest and waist height don't collide with other geometry.

Settling on a slight tilt, with the quiver's bottom near the right hip around x=-0.17 and top swinging toward x=-0.07, giving roughly a 12° lean.

The arrow fletching rises past the shoulder behind the head for a clean silhouette, and I'm nudging the quiver rightward so it doesn't overlap with the cape edge. Now I'm thinking through body details like a belt with a gold leaf buckle, a pouch, a dagger sheath at the hip, and possibly tassels or a sash at the waist.

Next I'm planning extruded tunic skirt panels flaring front and back from the belt, checking that they clear the thighs without rigidly binding to leg motion, then adding gold filigree decals — vine patterns on the chest and cloak, plus hem trim bands.

Beyond the decals, I'm budgeting part count and triangle limits, keeping sweep segments low to stay under 60k tris. For the face, I'm planning separate pieces for eyes, brows, nose, and a jointed jaw so the mouth can open, with the jaw hinge placed near the chin.

The jaw is a lower ellipsoid overlapping the cranium ellipsoid at the seam, with a small dark mouth sweep and tiny pinkish lip detail, no teeth needed. I'm working out precise head geometry numbers now -- defining the cranium and jaw ellipsoid centers and radii to position the face correctly.

Actually, a sphere-intersection approach leaves an awkward crease at the cheeks, so I'm switching to a lofted stack of cross-section stations from crown to chin, each with its own width and height, to get a smoother, more natural face profile.

Splitting it into two lofts — a cranium piece from crown to cheek, and a jaw piece from cheek to chin — joined near the cheekbone would create a visible seam, but since that seam lands close to the mouth line it should read as a fairly natural jaw contour.

For the eyes, I need to decal them onto the head's curved surface, so I'm thinking of projecting them using a hit-test approach—placing them at an azimuth/elevation around the center, roughly ±22° apart, computing their x-offset from that angle.

I'm sizing the eyes around 0.052×0.07, centered at x=±0.05, which gives a small gap between inner corners and leaves room for outward lash flicks near the face edge. Since the animeEye already includes brows and blush, I don't need to add separate brow decals.

For the remaining features, I'm planning a tiny nose sphere, a small curved mouth sweep in dark rose, and a skin-toned neck sweep spanning the visible neck length. For the boots, I'm sketching a sweep path from heel to ball to toe tip with a tapering radius function to shape the foot.

Working out the leg chain geometry: hip at y=0.95 down to ankle at y=0.11 gives roughly 0.84 vertical span against bone lengths of 0.45 and 0.43, leaving a natural slight bend. From the ankle I'm routing the foot forward and down through a ball joint around (0.13, 0.04, 0.12) to a toe tip near (0.12, 0.03, 0.24), shaping the sweep path for the boot.

I decide to figure out the foot sweep skinning by assigning bones per segment -- heel section tied to the ankle joint, toe section tied to the ball joint -- and plan to just write the code, typecheck it, and iterate visually rather than overthink it, referencing how chains are used for fingers and hands. I'm setting up a vector helper and starting to lay out shoulder joint coordinates for a slender anime-style frame.

For the arms I'm computing elbow and wrist positions from shoulder joints using normalized direction vectors and set lengths for upper arm and forearm, bending them forward and slightly outward to get natural elf-like long limbs, then placing the hand position and a rough palm-normal direction so the fist can wrap around a bow grip.

I'm estimating the fist curl geometry: given a grip diameter of roughly 0.035, I'm figuring the radius of the finger curl circle so that the finger segments wrap around it in an arc that sums close to full finger length, placing the grip center relative to the knuckle and palm-normal direction.

Now I'm computing the finger segment endpoints by summing each segment's length and direction vector progressively, tracking the running position along the d and pn axes to find where the fingertip lands.

I'm checking whether these positions stay the right distance from the bow grip's center, verifying the finger curls around the grip radius plus its own thickness so it wraps naturally without clipping into the grip.

Now I'm working out the finger spacing and orientation along the grip: four digits stacked along the grip's length, computing the cross product to get the direction perpendicular to the grip axis so I can place the index finger closest to the thumb side.

Still placing the thumb geometry...

I'm shaping the palm as a box or frustum with width spanning the finger base, oriented along the hand's forward direction with the curl axis perpendicular.

For the right hand, I'm mirroring the pose — defining forearm direction, hand direction, and palm normal as rough world vectors for a relaxed open posture.

Setting up the finger joint chains now, attaching each finger's segments to the wrist joint with tapered radii for a natural tapering look.

Now I'm counting up the full joint hierarchy: legs with hip-knee-ankle-ball chains, spine segments, neck and head, arms with clavicle-shoulder-elbow-wrist chains, and finger joints totaling around 28-30 for both hands, plus braid and cape joints for the extra details.

Skipping the jaw and cape joints for now since they'd be rigid on the spine, adding simple ear joints for the elf ears, and letting the bow ride rigidly on the left wrist rather than giving it its own rig -- bringing the total to roughly 60 joints.

Before placing exact coordinates I want to verify the builder API shapes like loft station options and the catmull spline helper, then start writing the actual TypeScript file importing the builder, math helpers, and other utilities needed for the rig.

Now I'm working out the color palette using cel-shaded paints -- warm pink skin tones, silvery lavender hair with possible teal-tinted gradient tips, and I'm about to define the tunic colors next.

Still picking the palette...

Plotting the bow's curve relative to the grip point, with an S-shaped limb profile so the tips angle back toward the archer for that elegant recurve silhouette.

Now I'm shaping the limb geometry with tapering radius from grip to tips, adding leather-and-gold wrapped handle details and wood grain texturing, then adding a thin string rod stretched between the tips.

For the quiver, I'm lathing a leather-walled shell profile from base to rim with gold decorative rings, positioning its axis between a bottom and top point near the archer's hip.

Now I'm placing seven arrows inside the quiver, spacing them in a circular cross-section with slight angular fan, giving each a pale wooden shaft, and adding crossed feather-card fletching near the nock end.

For the strap, I'm draping a rough path over the torso surface and sweeping a flat box section across it for the baldric, hoping the orientation transport doesn't twist too much. For the tunic, I'm planning a cel-shaded paint with gold trim lines positioned procedurally at the neckline, hem, and center front based on surface position.

I'm now thinking through gold stripe placement near the torso centerline and under-chest side panels, and deciding to use decals for the filigree and stripe details instead of pure procedural paint. I'm sketching out a gold vine filigree decal for the chest, rendered with alpha cutout against a transparent background.

For the cloak, I'm opting to skip decals entirely and instead paint the hem band directly using surface coordinates—gold trim plus a zigzag leaf pattern and thin ink outlines along the edge.

For the bracers, I'll add simple gold line bands using the same paint-on-sweep technique with t/degree coordinates. For hair locks, I'm extruding flat lock shapes and painting lighter highlight streaks and gradient tips onto them for texture, and considering leaf-shaped decals for the pauldron.

Now I need to nail down build order and coordinate conventions, defining a side helper where 1 means left and -1 means right. Before writing the detailed code, I want to double-check the actual API signatures for loft, sweep, and cards (options like color, bone, sides, section) by checking the builder type declarations.

input.command: ls; ls samples | head -3; ls scratch 2>/dev/null; grep -n "loft(" src/*.ts | head; grep -n "export type LoftStation\|export type TubeOptions\|export type SweepOptions" -A25 src/builder.ts | head -120
